What we supply

Aggregates and sand
Crushed stone in the graded sizes that concrete and road bases need, and sand, from quarries within the district. Our transport partners bring aggregate from quarries as far as 40 km away.
Cement
The grade and type the specification calls for. On this coast that usually means a blended cement, for the reasons set out on Civil and structural works.
Reinforcement steel
From approved mills, with the mill’s test certificate for every lot.
Structural and fabricated steel
Sections, plates and fabricated items, sequenced to the erection plan.
Construction consumables
Admixtures, grouts, curing compounds, cover blocks and the small things a site stops for when they run out.

Tested before it is used

Material quality is the first of the four controls in our quality loop.

  • Cement, aggregates and reinforcement steel are sourced from approved vendors.
  • They are tested at NABL-accredited laboratories before use.
  • A lot that fails is rejected, even when the truck is already at the gate.
  • Test reports go into the handover file.

Kept properly on a salt coast

Good material can be spoiled between the gate and the pour.

Cement
Stored dry and off the floor, used in the order it arrived. Cement that has taken up moisture is not used in structural concrete.
Steel
Stacked off the ground and covered. In this air an uncovered bar begins to rust within days, and loose rust and salt must be cleaned off before it is fixed.
Aggregates
Kept on clean hard-standing, by size, and washed if they carry dust or salt.
Water
Mixing and curing water is tested. Groundwater near this shore is often saline and cannot be assumed fit.

With the work, or without it

Most of our supply travels inside our own contracts. Where a client or another contractor wants material only, delivered to a programme, we supply it under a rate agreement with weighbridge records for every load.

What is coming

We are laying the groundwork for a ready-mix concrete facility and a structural steel fabrication yard in the Rajula belt. See The road ahead.

What one call can set in motion

Civil works. Mechanical erection. Shutdown and emergency maintenance. Heavy machinery with operators. Skilled and general manpower. Engineering review. Transport and heavy haulage. Staff, officer and site vehicles. Materials from approved sources.

Separately or together, from one firm.

The core

About 130 specialists: project managers, site engineers, millwright fitters, welders, electricians, riggers, masons and operators. They plan the work, supervise it and answer for it.

Machines

More than 300 machines, owned by people within thirty kilometres who know the plants and answer their phones.

Hands

More than 600 tradesmen on the call-up register, tested before they are listed and ready within 72 hours.

Engineers

Consulting engineers and approved suppliers, brought in when the drawing needs a second pair of eyes.

Wheels

Tippers, flatbeds, low-loaders, bulk carriers, buses and cars, from owners who have run this corridor for years.

One contract

All of it reaches the client as one order, one project manager and one invoice.

What it looks like in practice

For one plant expansion we coordinated the delivery of 800 tonnes of reinforcement steel, the deployment of two piling rigs and the arrival of 150 workers, all through our network, without a single phone call to the client.

Consider what did not happen on that job. The client’s engineer did not ring a steel stockist to ask where a trailer was. Nobody at the plant negotiated with a rig owner about shifting charges. No one arranged gate passes for 150 strangers one at a time. The steel, the rigs and the people were three lines in one plan, and the plan had one owner.

How a composite job is governed

  1. One order

    The scope is written once, with its parts priced so that you can see them.

  2. One project manager

    With authority over every part: the pour, the lift, the crew and the truck.

  3. One schedule

    A baseline with resources against every line. When the excavation slips a day, the rebar delivery moves with it, because the same person moves both.

  4. One report

    Daily. Progress across the whole job on a single page.

  5. One invoice

    Consolidated, with the measurement and the records behind it.

When one door is not the right door

We would be poor advisers if we told you it always was.

If you have a strong project team of your own and long relationships with specialist vendors, a single line from our schedule may serve you better than the whole of it. Hire the crane. Take the shutdown crew. Leave the rest as it is.

We are content to be one of your vendors. We would simply like to be the one you never have to chase.

Because the gap between trades is where projects go wrong.

Fitting a camera at a weighbridge needs a pole foundation, a trench, a duct, a cable, a power point, a mounting, a network port and a program. On most sites that is five contractors and a great many phone calls. On ours it is one line in the schedule.

This is the same idea as the rest of the firm. See The Zero-Interference Doctrine.

Site-office IT
Connection, computers, printing, attendance and document control for a project office. See Site-office IT.
Networks
Fibre, copper and radio links across a plant or a site. See Networks and cameras.
Cameras
Gates, weighbridges, yards and work fronts, with storage. See Networks and cameras.
Weighbridge systems
Unattended weighing with cameras, barriers and tamper checks. See Weighbridge systems.
Fleet tracking
Position, trips, fuel and driving for tippers, tankers and buses. See Fleet tracking.
Access and attendance
Gate passes, induction records and biometric attendance, joined to the wage register.

Security

Who does the work

ATKAYVA is a network organisation. We do not pretend to employ every skill.

  1. Our project manager owns it

    The same single accountable face as on a civil job. See Project governance.

  2. Our crews do the physical work

    Foundations, trenches, ducts, cable pulling, poles, panels, earthing and power.

  3. Proven specialists do the specialist work

    Network engineers, system integrators and software people join the network the way a crane owner does: tested on a small job before they are trusted with a large one. See The standard.

  4. One hand-over

    Drawings of what was laid and where, passwords in a sealed envelope, and a person to call.

What a site office needs

A connection
Two different routes to the internet, so that one failing does not stop the day. Mobile data from two networks at the least, and fibre where the plant can lend it.
Wi-Fi
In the office, the stores and the canteen. Not on the work front, where a phone is a hazard.
Computers
Rugged enough for dust. Backed up every night without anyone remembering to.
Printing
Permits, drawings and pour cards are still paper at the work front. A printer that fails is a stopped job.
Attendance
A reader at the gate that records who came in, joined to the wage register. See Our people.
Document control
One place where the current revision of every drawing lives, and the old ones are marked old.
Power
A battery backup that carries the office through a changeover without losing a file.
A screen
The day’s plan, the permits open and the weather, where everyone can see them. See Live boards.

Set up with the rest of the site

The office goes up with the fence and the stores. It is not something to be sorted out in week three.

  1. Before mobilisation

    We ask what your plant’s rules are: which networks we may join, what may be photographed, what may leave the gate.

  2. Day one

    Connection, printer, attendance reader and the document store are working when the crew arrives.

  3. Every day

    Backups run. Attendance flows to the time office. The day’s reports go out from the same place every evening.

  4. At demobilisation

    Records are handed over, devices are wiped, and nothing of yours leaves in a drawer.

Dust, heat and salt

This is the Saurashtra coast. Office equipment made for an air-conditioned floor in a city lasts one summer here.

  • Enclosures are sealed against limestone dust.
  • Nothing sensitive stands in direct sun. In May the afternoon is forty-one degrees outside the container.
  • Connectors are chosen and greased for salt air. See What salt does to concrete.

The problem

A weighbridge is where a load becomes money. So it is where people are tempted.

The old tricks are well known. A wheel left off the platform. A driver who stays in the cab for the gross weight and steps out for the tare. A slip written by hand. A second weighing that nobody recorded. We wrote about it in The weighbridge.

What the system does

  1. The truck is recognised

    A tag on the windscreen or a camera reading the number plate identifies the vehicle. Nobody types it.

  2. The truck is placed

    Sensors confirm that every axle is on the platform before the weight is taken.

  3. The weight is taken

    Directly from the indicator. No keyboard is involved.

  4. The truck is photographed

    Front, rear and top of the load, stamped with the weight and the time.

  5. The slip is made

    Printed, sent to the buyer and the transporter at the same moment, and stored.

  6. The barrier lifts

    Only when the record is complete.

What a tracker tells you

Where
Every vehicle on a map, now and for any hour in the past.
Trips

Waiting
How long each truck stood at the gate, the weighbridge and the hopper. Queues become visible.
Speed
Every stretch driven above the limit, with the place and the time.

Level in the tank over time. A sudden drop while the engine is off is not evaporation.

Fences on the map

The lion roads

Asiatic lions cross the roads between Rajula, Pipavav and Jafrabad after dark. We already tell our drivers to slow down on those roads at night. See Lion country.

A tracker can hold us to it. The stretches are fenced on the map, the night limit is set, and any vehicle that breaks it is reported to the coordinator the same hour.

A rule that is measured is a rule that is kept.

Shift buses

For a shift bus the question is only one: did it reach the gate before the shift? The tracker answers that for every bus and every day, and tells the people waiting at a stop how far away it is. See Staff and shift transport.

What drivers should know

  • The tracker is fitted openly and every driver is told what it records.
  • It records the vehicle, not the man’s private life. It is not carried in a pocket.
  • The records protect a careful driver. When a transporter is accused of a missing trip, the map settles it.

A clerk’s infected laptop can then reach the system that runs the mill. The two should be separated, with one guarded door between them.
Shared passwords
One password for the whole shift, written on the monitor.
No backups, or backups never tested
The day you need one is not the day to find out.
Old remote-access tools
Left by a vendor years ago, and still listening.
USB sticks
The oldest route into a control room.
Contractors’ laptops
Ours included. They are plugged in for a day, and nobody checks what came with them.
Payment emails
A message that looks like a supplier’s and asks you to change the bank account.

The last one first

The commonest loss is not a clever attack on a control system. It is an email.

Somebody writes in a supplier’s name, with a new bank account. The invoice is real. The account is not.

Our own rule is on Fraud alert: bank details are sent only on our letterhead and confirmed by telephone on the number published on the Contact page. We recommend the same rule to every client for every supplier.

What we offer

  1. A walk-through

    Half a day with your electrical and IT people. We look at how the networks are arranged, who can reach what, and how backups are taken. You get a plain list, most important first.

  2. The physical fixes

    Separate cabinets and cabling for office and plant networks. Locked ports. Lockable panels. These are our kind of work.

  3. The specialist fixes

    Firewalls, backup systems and access controls, fitted by proven specialists in the network under our project manager.

  4. The habits

    A short talk for the people who use the systems, in the language they use. Most security is habit.

Our own conduct on your network

  • We connect nothing to a plant network without written permission.
  • Our laptops are checked before they come through your gate.
  • We ask for the least access that will do the job, and we hand it back at the end.
  • Anything we learn about your systems is covered by the confidentiality we owe you for everything else. See Why no client is named.

Seeing

It watches camera pictures and notices what a tired eye misses at three in the morning: a head without a helmet, a person inside a barrier, a truck reversing towards a group.

Reading

It reads drawings, bills of quantities, tenders and permits. It pulls out quantities, compares revisions and finds the clause you were looking for.

Noticing

It watches vibration, temperature and current. It learns what normal looks like for one particular machine, and says when today is not normal.

It can flag a risk. It cannot weigh it against a schedule, a client and a crew. A person decides.

Under a suspended load, behind a reversing vehicle, inside a guarded machine.

What happens next

  1. The system flags it

  2. A named person is told

  3. He looks, and acts

Reads title blocks, schedules and notes. Compares one revision with the next and lists what moved.

Procedures
Turns a shelf of manuals into something a person can ask a question of.

In three languages

Most of the people who do the work on this coast read Gujarati or Hindi more easily than English. Most procedures are written in English.

A procedure can be put into all three and read aloud on a phone. The safety signs on our sites already carry three languages. The instructions behind them should too. See ગુજરાતી and हिन्दी.

The rule of the second reader

Nothing a machine has read reaches a price, a drawing or a permit until an engineer has checked it against the page.

The machine shows where it found each figure. The engineer looks at that place. This is faster than reading everything, and safer than trusting anything.

  1. Friday evening

    A tender is issued. Four hundred pages, six drawings, a bill of quantities with three hundred lines.

  2. Friday night

    The machine produces a list: scope, quantities, dates, unusual clauses, documents required, questions to ask.

  3. Saturday morning

    An engineer spends two hours checking that list against the pages, not two days finding it.

    The site visit is planned around the questions that matter.

The idea

Every rotating machine has a signature. A fan, a mill drive, a gearbox, a conveyor pulley: each one shakes and warms in its own way when it is healthy. A sensor records that. A program learns it. When the signature changes, somebody is told.

What is watched

Vibration
The first sign of a failing bearing, a loose foundation bolt or a rotor going out of balance.
Temperature
Bearings, windings, gearbox oil, kiln shell.
Current
A motor working harder than it did last month for the same load.
Sound
Sometimes the ear of an old fitter, recorded.

Why it matters most before a shutdown

A plant’s annual shutdown is a fixed window. Every job in it was put on a list weeks before. See The shutdown playbook.

The worst thing that can happen is a discovery. You open a gearbox on day six and find what you should have known on day minus thirty. Then you need a part that is in another state, and the kiln stays cold while it travels.

Monitoring through the year turns discoveries into line items.

AspectWithout itWith it
A bearing on the raw mill fanFails in service. Unplanned stop.Flagged six weeks early. Changed in the shutdown.
The shutdown listBuilt from memory and inspectionBuilt from a year of readings
SparesOrdered in a hurryOrdered in time
After the shutdownHopeThe same sensors confirm the repair

What it needs to work

A known machine
Its speed, its bearings, its history.
Time
It learns what normal is. The first weeks are for listening.
Good mounting
A sensor on a loose bracket measures the bracket.
Somebody who acts
An alert that nobody owns is noise.

What we do

We fit and cable the sensors, and we do the mechanical work they point to. Alignment, grouting, bearing changes and foundation repairs are our ordinary trade. See Alignment and grouting. The analysis comes from specialists in the network.

That closes a loop most plants leave open. The firm that hears the fault is the firm that fixes it.

Start with five machines

Not the whole plant. The five whose failure stops production. Thirty days of listening, and one report. See Start with a pilot.
